subtype: Approach: writing a list from the teacher's notice [Action]
passage:
Monday. The circular about the museum trip came home in Tarun's bag. He read it twice at the study table, pen in hand.
Tuesday. He copied each item onto a slip: lunch box, water bottle, cap, ID card, fifty rupees. He did not add his football, because the notice never asked for it.
Friday. The bus left at seven. At the gate, Ira Ma'am checked each child and paused at Tarun's bag. "Everything the notice asks for. Good." Tarun grinned and climbed aboard.

qa.q: What items did Tarun write on his slip?
qa.a: He wrote lunch box, water bottle, cap, ID card and fifty rupees.

qa.q: What was Tarun thinking when he left his football off the list?
qa.a: Tarun felt sure and confident, because the notice showed what was needed, so there was no reason to guess.

qa.q: What could Tarun do if part of the circular seemed unclear, and why?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher or a parent to read it with him, since the notice is the source and a second reader can confirm it.

qa.q: How does Ira Ma'am see Tarun's bag at the gate?
qa.a: She sees a child who followed what the notice asked, and she says "Good", so she can move on quickly.

grounding: A boy reads the school notice and builds his packing list from what it states, without guessing.

subtype: Approach: writing a list from the teacher's notice [Action]
passage: Yusuf, you want to know why your Ujjwal Chacha still reads every notice twice? Because of the museum trip, when I was a boy. The school gave us a paper circular. Most boys stuffed it in their bags. I sat on the steps and read it slowly. Packed lunch. Water bottle. Cap. School ID card. Twenty rupees for the entry ticket. I copied the five things on the back of my hand in ink, and at home onto a slip of paper. Next morning my friend Pappu forgot his ID and had to wait with the teacher at the gate. I didn't guess anything, beta. The notice told me what to bring, and I brought it.

qa.q: What was the twenty rupees for?
qa.a: It was for the entry ticket.

qa.q: How did young Ujjwal feel the next morning compared with Pappu?
qa.a: Young Ujjwal probably felt relieved and a bit proud, since Pappu had to wait at the gate while Ujjwal had everything.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference, and what else could have helped?
qa.a: Reading the circular slowly and copying the list was the key choice; Ujjwal could also have shown the list to a parent to double-check.

qa.q: How might Pappu have felt waiting with the teacher at the gate?
qa.a: Pappu probably felt embarrassed and left out while the others went in.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy, making a packing list from the school's trip notice so he did not have to guess.

subtype: Approach: writing a list from the teacher's notice [Action]
passage: The circular for the planetarium trip came home in Deepak's bag on a rainy Thursday, and by the time he found it, the ink had run. His mother, Rehana, was on a late shift, and the trip was the next morning. Deepak spread the soggy paper on the table and read what he could. "Packed lunch. Water. Cap... is that cap? ID card. Fifty rupees." He wrote each item on a clean sheet, then held the circular under the lamp to check the smudged word. It was cap. He packed each thing and ticked it off. When his mother came home at ten, the bag was by the door with the list on top. She read it, and then read the circular. "You didn't guess anything," she said.

qa.q: Why was the ink on the circular smudged?
qa.a: It was a rainy day and the ink had run.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when his mother read the list?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and relieved that he had managed it himself.

qa.q: What else could Deepak do if a word on the circular was unreadable?
qa.a: He could call a classmate or check the class message group with his mother's help, rather than guess.

qa.q: How does the packed bag look to Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana, tired after a late shift, is pleased and impressed that Deepak used the notice carefully.

grounding: It shows a boy using the teacher's circular to write a packing list so he does not have to guess.
